UrbanMart Holdings - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the UrbanMart Holdings Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, participants are required to use their handsets to mute any background noise. Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Emily Carter, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter, Head of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss UrbanMart Holdings' results for the third quarter of 2024. Joining me on today’s call are Jamie Lawson, Chief Executive Officer; and Raj Singh, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to Jamie.

Jamie Lawson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Emily. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report UrbanMart Holdings' strong performance for the third quarter. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment marked by persistent inflation, softening consumer confidence, and shifting spending patterns toward value-oriented categories.

In Q3, we advanced our Retail Reimagined strategy across omnichannel acceleration, store footprint optimization, supply chain resilience, and customer-centric innovation. Omnichannel sales reached 28% of e-commerce revenue, digital sales hit $1.2 billion or 18% of total revenue, and our new NextGen stores posted impressive comps. Store productivity improved, with square-foot sales at $620, and our Rewards program drove higher engagement.

E-commerce growth was robust, fueled by our app enhancements like AR try-on and RFID smart carts, alongside partnerships for same-day delivery. Store performance varied regionally but overall strengthened, with Southeast comps at 7.2% and remodels boosting inventory turns. Our marketing initiatives around personalization and sustainability lifted repeat purchases and basket sizes.

We are confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Raj to provide more details on our financial results.

Raj Singh, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, Jamie. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for the third quarter of 2024. Our total revenue for the quarter was $8.1 billion, a 4.5% increase compared to the same period last year, driven by comp store sales growth of 3.2%, new store openings, and digital channel expansion. Gross margin expanded to 36.4%, up 110 basis points year-over-year, primarily driven by supply chain efficiencies, lower markdowns, higher private-label penetration, and progress on shrink mitigation. Operating expenses were $2.0 billion, representing 24.7% of revenue, reflecting disciplined cost controls and productivity gains. Net income was $520 million, or $0.98 per diluted share. We generated $680 million in cash flow from operations, underscoring our strong cash generation. Inventory levels are currently optimized at 12 weeks of supply, with turnover improving to 5.8 times, supporting our margin expansion.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

Before we dive deeper, let me provide a detailed update on our key strategic initiatives, which continue to drive our transformation as a leading brick-and-mortar retailer in the general merchandise and home goods sectors. Our Retail Reimagined strategy—launched two years ago—focuses on four pillars: omnichannel acceleration, store footprint optimization, supply chain resilience, and customer-centric innovation. We've made significant progress across all areas, delivering tangible results amid this tough macro backdrop.

Starting with omnichannel acceleration, our top priority to connect physical and digital retail. In Q3, omnichannel sales—including buy-online-pick-up-in-store, ship-from-store, and curbside—made up 28% of total e-commerce revenue, rising from 22% last year and 18% in Q3 2022. This outperforms peers like Target, where BOPIS reached 25% last quarter. Our BOPIS fulfillment now exceeds 95% within two hours at 85% of stores, powered by investments in micro-fulfillment centers. We've implemented ShipBob-style automation in 45 high-volume sites, cutting order cycle times by 40% and enabling same-day fulfillment for 62% of requests. Digital sales rose 15% year-over-year to $1.2 billion, or 18% of total revenue, keeping us on pace for 20% by fiscal 2025. Our updated UrbanMart app, with AR try-on for apparel and furniture, has increased conversions by 32% for those features. In addition, RFID-enabled smart carts are being piloted in 20 Chicago-area stores—much like Walmart's approach—lifting average basket size by 12% via personalized upsells.

On store footprint optimization, we're right-sizing our portfolio for maximum productivity. We opened 18 new NextGen stores this quarter—compact 25,000-square-foot urban prototypes with experiential elements like local vendor pop-ups, interactive demo kitchens for small appliances, and EV charging—bringing the total to 62. These locations are seeing early comparable sales 22% above our fleet average, appealing strongly to millennials and Gen Z who value experiences. Meanwhile, we closed 42 underperforming big-box stores in low-density Midwest markets, generating $180 million in proceeds for remodels and debt paydown. This has boosted overall store productivity by 8%, with sales per square foot now at $620, up from $575 a year ago. Regionally, Southeast comps jumped 7.2% on housing turnover and back-to-school strength, while Midwest comps eased to 1.8% from auto strike effects on discretionary spend—patterns echoed at Kohl's and Macy's. We're on track to remodel 150 legacy stores by year-end, adding open-sell flooring for home goods that raised inventory turns to 5.2 times from 4.1 times, plus self-checkout kiosks trimming transaction times by 25%.

Our supply chain resilience efforts are paying off big in this volatile world. We've shifted to 65% North American sourcing from 48% two years back, minimizing ocean freight risks from Red Sea issues. Our new 1.2 million-square-foot Dallas-Fort Worth DC, inspired by Home Depot's setups, has reduced lead times by 28% and out-of-stocks to 3.2% from 7.1% in Q3 2022. This supports the 110 basis point gross margin gain to 36.4%, via fewer markdowns and private-label sales at 42%—with Urban Essentials up 24%, beating national brands. AI demand forecasting from Blue Yonder delivers 92% accuracy on seasonal items, vital amid tariff pressures on apparel, where we've hedged 70% of fiscal 2024 exposure.

Customer-centric innovation and loyalty are ramping up engagement too. UrbanMart Rewards has 45 million active members, with 68% redemption—beating the 55% industry average per Deloitte. Machine learning personalization has boosted repeat buys by 19%, with targeted campaigns driving 14% of Q3 traffic. In-store Beacon tech pushes notifications for 25% higher baskets in high-margin kitchenware. Our Green Thread program, with 30% recycled apparel sourcing, improved Net Promoter Scores by 15 points among eco-shoppers, mirroring Patagonia and REI trends. DoorDash partnerships for same-day delivery in 15 MSAs captured 8% urban market share, adding $75 million in revenue.

Regionally, we're customizing: Northeast relocations to edge-city formats countered high rents for 5.9% comps despite foot traffic dips. Sunbelt growth shines with 12 new Florida/Texas stores at 9.4%, tied to migration and home improvement like Lowe's. Our Mexico JV with Liverpool hit breakeven in nine months across 20 stores, with 11% comps, eyeing 50 by 2027.

These efforts back our fiscal 2024 guidance of 4-6% total sales growth, 3-5% comps, and adjusted EBITDA margins of 8.2-8.7%. Capex holds at $850 million for quick-payback projects under 24 months. This sets us to outperform in consolidation, like Costco and TJX.

Next, as we examine factors shaping our margins, I'd like to address a persistent challenge: inventory shrink, especially theft, which pressured gross margins this quarter much like it has for peers at Target and Walmart. Our consolidated gross margin landed at 36.4%, down slightly in spots but up overall year-over-year. Of the dynamics at play, about 45 basis points of pressure stemmed from higher shrink—around 40% of any compression. For full-year 2023, shrink was 1.75% of net sales, versus 1.45% in 2022 and a pre-pandemic 1.3%. That equated to $285 million in losses on $16.3 billion in sales.

Theft drives 65% of shrink, with admin errors at 20%, vendor issues at 10%, and internal fraud at 5%. External theft and organized retail crime—or ORC—dominate, hitting consumer electronics like AirPods and chargers, prestige beauty such as La Mer, and seasonal apparel for over 55% of losses. Q3 ORC incidents rose 22% year-over-year, aligning with the National Retail Federation's 2023 survey showing industry shrink at 1.6% and ORC costing $112 billion yearly.

Impacts differ by region: Urban California markets with over 150 stores saw 2.4% shrink rates, 60 basis points above average, fueled by Prop 47 enabling smash-and-grabs on appliances and tools. Midwest and Southeast like Texas and Ohio held at 1.5%, aided by enforcement. Our 80 Canadian stores stayed at 1.6% via RCMP ties, watching U.S. border risks.

We're countering aggressively—loss prevention gets $65 million of our $250 million 2024 capex. AI video analytics from Everseen in 450 of 1,200 U.S. stores cut theft 18% in pilots, spotting anomalies like sweethearting or concealments at 95% accuracy, linked to Eagle Eye. RFID tags now cover 70% of high-shrink SKUs by year-end, from 35%, dropping shrink 25% in electronics like Macy's and Lowe's. We've shifted 30% of self-checkouts to assisted biometric lanes against 30% industry SCO fraud rise. Operationally, NRF task force and DA partnerships in LA/SF yielded 1,200 ORC arrests YTD, up 40%.

We see shrink moderating to 1.65% in late 2024 for 20-25 basis point margin help, assuming execution and Prop 47 tweaks. Conservatively, holiday peaks could add 30-40 bps pressure if theft spikes to 2.1% like Q4 2023. Overall, our tech and partnerships aim to beat averages, targeting 29%+ margins by 2026 with shrink under 1.4%.

Turning to inventory optimization, another core lever in our brick-and-mortar operations against Amazon and Wayfair. We've cut excess inventory 28% year-over-year, fueling 210 basis points of gross margin expansion this quarter. Inventory turnover hit 5.8 times from 4.2 times, days on hand at 63 from 87—topping NRF's 4.9 times specialty average, matching Home Depot's 6.2 times. Shrink fell 12% to 1.1% of sales, stockouts for top SKUs dropped to 3.5% from 8%, lifting in-stocks to 96% and conversions 2.2 points.

Our approach layers analytics, partnerships, and execution. AI demand forecasting via Blue Yonder across 1,200 stores uses POS, weather, and macro data. In home décor—22% of sales—it flagged 15% Midwest back-to-school demand for pillows/rugs, dodging 18% markdowns. Accuracy reached 92% SKU-week, trimming safety stock 20% at 98% fill rates for apparel.

Just-in-time via vendor-managed inventory covers 65% with Mohawk flooring and Tempur-Pedic bedding—vendors hold title till POS pull, slashing freight 14% and backroom excess 35%, key for 8x-turnover kitchen items.

ABC/XYZ classification with Manhattan WMS tags A-items (10% SKUs, 70% sales like private cookware) via RFID for 99.9% accuracy; B/C use sampling, cutting inventory costs $12 million to $7.5 million. IoT in 40% DCs guards perishables, saving $2.8 million spoilage.

Regionally tuned: Northeast's 350 stores use Instacart BOPIS hubs, cutting excess 32%, outerwear stockouts 22%. Sunbelt Southwest's 280 stores apply dynamic pricing on aged outdoor furniture, trimming markdowns 17% at 150%+ GMROI.

This frees $450 million working capital for 150 remodels with digital planograms, cuts landfill 25% for eco-appeal (62% shoppers per Deloitte). Q4 expands AI for Black Friday 25% surge on 10% inventory, pilots IBM blockchain for electronics shrink. Diversified sourcing (45% domestic) buffers Red Sea risks. This added $0.14 to Q3 EPS, sets 200+ bps gains ahead—making inventory our moat.

Finally, our forward-looking guidance for Q4 and full fiscal 2024 reflects disciplined execution in moderating inflation, value spending resilience, and e-comm/discounter rivalry. For Q4, net sales of $8.45 billion to $8.65 billion, 3-5% growth versus $8.25 billion last year—2% new square footage, 1% closure drag. Comps 3-4%, with 2-3% traffic from Store of the Future remodels like interactive kiosks and beauty bars akin to Target-Ulta, plus 100 bps conversion via Rewards app (45 million members, +15% YoY).

Q4 gross margin 38.2-38.7%, +50-100 bps from Q3's 37.8% on supply chain, private labels at 28% (up from 24%), 20% lower freight, 3-5% landed cost cuts—though holiday promos like 2023 Black Friday may trim 30 bps. SG&A 24.5-24.8% of sales, +20 bps YoY on scheduling tech (15% less overtime), milder utilities. Operating income $1.05-$1.15 billion, adjusted EPS $1.52-$1.62 at 25.5% tax, 650 million shares.

Full FY2024: sales $32.1-$32.6 billion, 2.5-4% growth, comps 2.2-3% (up from prior 1.5-2.5%), led by home +4.5%, essentials +3.2%, apparel +1%. Gross margin 37.9-38.3%, +40 bps on 10-week inventory (from 12), 60% RFID shrink cuts. Adjusted EPS $5.25-$5.45 (prior $5.00-$5.30), with $150 million savings from Fleet Optimization 2.0: 25 closures, 15 Sunbelt urban opens. Capex $1.2 billion—40% remodels (150 stores), 30% micro-fulfillment for 18% BOPIS digital share (+40% YoY), 20% digital.

Sunbelt comps 4-5% on migration/traffic/seasonal patio; Northeast/Midwest flat to +1% on weather/delinqs; West +2.5% via artisan privates. Into 2025, digital to 22%, GenAI pricing lifts sell-through 5%; 55% U.S. sourcing resilient vs. unemployment/tariffs. Clean inventories, $4.2 billion op cash, $2.5 billion liquidity.

This drives profitable growth, outpacing Macy's/Kohl's via value, experiences, efficiency.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. As a reminder, participants are required to use handsets to mute background noise. Our first question comes from Laura Bennett with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Laura Bennett (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of shrink and theft on your sales and margins this quarter?

Jamie Lawson, Chief Executive Officer:
Good morning, Laura. Shrink and theft remain industry-wide pressures, but our multi-faceted response—including AI analytics, RFID expansion, and partnerships—has started to bend the curve, limiting it to 45 basis points of margin impact. We're seeing early wins like 18% theft reductions in pilots, and we expect moderation ahead as initiatives scale.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mike Rivera with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Mike Rivera (JPMorgan):
Thanks. What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

Raj Singh, Chief Financial Officer:
Thanks, Mike. For Q4, we're guiding comps to 3-4%, with traffic up 2-3% from remodel momentum and conversion gains via personalization. Regionally, Sunbelt strength offsets softer Northeast/Midwest, positioning us well for holiday acceleration.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Sarah Kim with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Sarah Kim (Morgan Stanley):
Good morning. On inventory optimization, how are you balancing stockouts with excess amid supply chain volatility?

Raj Singh, Chief Financial Officer:
Morning, Sarah. Our AI forecasting at 92% accuracy and 65% VMI keep stockouts at 3.5% while cutting excess 28%. Diversified sourcing and regional hubs like Northeast BOPIS mitigate risks, freeing capital for growth.

Operator:
Thank you. That concludes today's Q&A. I'll now turn it back over to the team for closing remarks.

Jamie Lawson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Emily Carter, Head of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.
